entities.name: Manius Acilius Glabrio Gnaeus Cornelius Severus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Manius Acilius Glabrio Gnaeus Cornelius Severus, a prominent senator of the Roman Empire, served as consul ordinarius in 152 CE alongside Marcus Valerius Homullus during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius. Born into the illustrious Acilia gens, a plebeian family that had risen to prominence in the Roman Republic and continued to hold significant influence in the Imperial period, Glabrio's career exemplifies the enduring power and intricate social networks of the Roman senatorial aristocracy. His life, largely reconstructed from epigraphic evidence, offers a window into the political and administrative structures of the High Roman Empire, a period of relative stability and prosperity known as the Pax Romana, even as the seeds of future imperial challenges were being sown.

The pinnacle of Acilius Glabrio's public service was his consulship, a position that marked the apex of a Roman senator's cursus honorum, signifying immense prestige and responsibility within the imperial administration. Beyond this singular achievement, inscriptions reveal his participation in the Quindecimviri sacris faciundis, one of the four major priestly colleges of Rome, indicating his involvement in state religious affairs and his high social standing. While specific administrative or military accomplishments are not extensively documented for Glabrio himself, his tenure as consul occurred at a time when the Roman Empire was at its territorial zenith, managing vast provinces from Britannia to Mesopotamia through a sophisticated bureaucratic and military apparatus.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Manius Acilius Glabrio Gnaeus Cornelius Severus's career as a Roman senator and consul in 152 CE provides a specific example of the Roman elite's administrative function during the High Empire, contributing to our understanding of prosopography and governance. While not a major historical figure, his documented offices illustrate the continuity of aristocratic power.
